title: Introduction to Embedded Systems
subtitle: What embedded systems are and how they differ from general-purpose computers
author: Kernal Team

whyItExists.problem: Modern devices — from smart watches to car ABS systems — need computers that run a single task reliably, indefinitely, with tiny power budgets and no operating system to get in the way.
whyItExists.solution: Embedded systems use a microcontroller (CPU + memory + I/O on one chip) running bare-metal or RTOS firmware, optimised for deterministic, low-power, real-time operation.
whyItExists.whenToUse: When you need: hardware control, real-time response, ultra-low power, mass production cost sensitivity, or a device without a display or keyboard.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: When you need a full OS, complex networking stacks, a GUI, or high computational throughput — use a Raspberry Pi or a PC instead.

explainModes.beginner: An embedded system is a tiny computer built into a device to do one job — like the chip in your microwave that tracks time and controls the magnetron. It has just enough memory and speed to do its job and nothing more.
explainModes.simple: Unlike a laptop that can run any app, an embedded system runs one dedicated program forever. It uses a microcontroller — a single chip with CPU, RAM, and storage — instead of separate components.
explainModes.standard: Embedded systems pair a microcontroller (MCU) with minimal RAM and flash to run firmware deterministically. They interact with the physical world through GPIO, ADC, timers, and bus peripherals like I2C and SPI.
explainModes.technical: MCUs run bare-metal or RTOS firmware in a super-loop or interrupt-driven model. They lack MMU and OS scheduling; every cycle counts. Real-time constraints are met through hardware timers and interrupt priority levels.
explainModes.deepDive: Embedded design involves trade-offs across power consumption (active vs sleep modes), memory hierarchy (flash/SRAM/EEPROM), clock speed, peripheral availability, and cost. Harvard architecture (separate program/data buses) enables single-cycle fetch; ARM Cortex-M uses a modified Harvard with unified address space. Bare-metal firmware relies on startup code (reset handler, vector table, .data/.bss initialisation) before main().

content.text: An embedded system is a computer designed for a specific purpose, embedded within a larger device. Unlike a laptop that runs arbitrary software, an embedded system executes dedicated firmware — the program is fixed and runs from power-on to power-off. Examples surround you: the ABS controller in your car, the thermostat on your wall, the chip inside a smart lightbulb.

a.name: Microcontroller (MCU)
a.description: CPU + RAM + Flash + peripherals on a single chip
a.useWhen: You need to control hardware with tight timing and low cost

b.name: Microprocessor (MPU)
b.description: CPU-only chip; needs external RAM, storage, and peripherals
b.useWhen: You need a full OS, GUI, or complex networking (use Raspberry Pi)

content.text: Embedded development follows a cycle: write firmware on your PC → compile to machine code → flash (upload) to the MCU via USB/JTAG → run & observe via serial monitor or LEDs → debug and repeat. The Arduino IDE and PlatformIO handle this cycle with one-click uploads.

Arduino is the best starting point for embedded programming. For production IoT, consider the ESP32 (built-in WiFi/Bluetooth) or STM32 (more powerful peripherals). Arduino-style programming works on all three.
Never connect 5V signals to a Raspberry Pi GPIO pin — it uses 3.3V logic and 5V will permanently damage the GPIO controller. Always check your board's voltage level before wiring sensors.

A key concept in embedded systems is real-time operation: the system must respond to events within a guaranteed time window. A car's ABS must respond to a wheel-slip event in under 10 ms — if it misses that window, the response is useless or dangerous. General-purpose computers (Linux, Windows) have no such guarantees because the OS scheduler can preempt your code at any moment.

content.definition: Missing a deadline is a system failure. Used in safety-critical systems: ABS, pacemakers, flight controls.
Missing a deadline degrades quality but doesn't cause failure. Example: video streaming — a late frame causes a glitch but not a crash.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a microcontroller and a microprocessor?
options: Microcontrollers include CPU, memory, and I/O peripherals on one chip
questions.explanation: A microcontroller integrates CPU, flash, RAM, and I/O on a single chip. A microprocessor is just the CPU — it needs external memory and peripherals.

questions.question: Which platform would you choose for a low-cost WiFi-enabled IoT sensor?
questions.explanation: The ESP32 has built-in WiFi and Bluetooth, 520 KB RAM, and runs at 240 MHz — purpose-built for IoT. Arduino Uno has no wireless capability.

questions.question: What is 'hard real-time' in an embedded system?
options: The system is physically hard to program
Missing a response deadline is a system failure
The firmware is compiled, not interpreted
questions.explanation: Hard real-time means every deadline must be met — missing one is unacceptable (e.g., ABS, pacemakers). Soft real-time allows occasional misses.

faq.a: No. The Arduino Uno has only 2 KB of SRAM and 32 KB of flash — far too little for Linux. Linux needs at least 4 MB RAM. Use a Raspberry Pi if you need a full OS.

faq.q: What language do you use for embedded programming?
faq.a: C and C++ are the standard. Arduino uses C++ with a simplified API. MicroPython brings Python to microcontrollers (ESP32, RP2040) but with a performance cost.

faq.q: What is the difference between Arduino Uno and ESP32?
faq.a: The ESP32 is far more powerful: 240 MHz dual-core vs 16 MHz, 520 KB RAM vs 2 KB, plus built-in WiFi and Bluetooth. ESP32 costs about the same ($3–5) but can't use all Arduino shields directly.
